summary: Changes the PIM Sparse Mode Join message format so a node can attach extra attributes when it joins a multicast tree. Before this there was no way to pass such additional information. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7887.

plainLanguage.summary: When you sign up for a newsletter, you may want to add notes like how you want it delivered. This lets a router add extra notes when it asks to join a multicast group.

subtitle: A way for a router to attach extra, typed attributes to a PIM Join message when it asks to join a multicast tree.

tldr.problem: A PIM Sparse Mode Join message names a multicast group and a source, but there was no way to say anything more about how the tree should be built.
tldr.mechanism: A new Encoded-Source Address encoding type, type 1, carries one or more Join Attributes in Type-Length-Value form. A new PIM Hello option tells neighbors that a router can parse them.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines only the container and the generic rules. It defines no particular attribute, and the attributes are only useful where every PIM router in the domain understands them. It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7887.

today: RFC 5384 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7887. Read the two together for the current rules.

sections.title: Why Joins Need Attributes
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode (RFC 4601), a Join message names the multicast distribution trees a router wants to join. Each tree is identified by a group address plus a source address, and the source may be a wild card. Sometimes it would help to say more about how the tree should be built, but until this RFC there was no way to do so.

The fix is a new encoding type for the Encoded-Source Address field. The only value defined in RFC 4601 is type 0. This RFC defines type 1, which may carry a sequence of Join Attributes, each encoded as a Type-Length-Value (TLV). Apart from the attributes, a type 1 address is identical to a type 0 address.

The RFC deliberately defines no particular attribute. It specifies how attributes are encoded into Join messages and the generic procedures common to all of them. PIM Dense Mode is not considered.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-up form for a multicast group used to have no space for notes. Now there is a notes box, but this paper only builds the box. It does not say what to write in it.

sections.title: The Type 1 Encoded-Source Address
sections.content:
The default source encoding has no room for an attribute field, so the RFC introduces encoding type 1. After the usual source address come the attributes, one after another. Each starts with two flag bits and a 6-bit type, followed by a one-octet length and then a value.

  • F-bit (transitive): if set, the attribute is transitive, otherwise it is non-transitive.
  • E-bit (end of attributes): set on the last attribute in the field. There is no count of attributes, so this bit marks the end.
  • Attr_Type: a 6-bit field naming the type of the attribute.
  • Length: the length in octets of the value field, as an unsigned binary integer.

A type 1 address MUST contain at least one attribute. To say that a tree has no attributes, a router uses a type 0 address. Attributes of the same or different types can appear several times in one field, and attributes of one type need not be contiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a little tag saying what kind it is and how long it is. The very last note gets a special mark so the reader knows when to stop.

sections.title: The Join Attribute Hello Option
sections.content:
A router that does not understand type 1 cannot process a Join that uses it. To avoid sending such a Join to the wrong neighbor, the RFC defines a PIM Hello option called Join Attribute, option type 26 with option length 0.

A router willing to receive type 1 addresses MUST include this option in its Hellos. A router MUST NOT send a type 1 address out any interface where a PIM neighbor has not included the option. Even a router that is not the upstream neighbor must be able to parse the packet, because it needs to do Join suppression or overriding.

The option says only that the router handles the encoding. It does not mean the router understands every attribute type, and there is no Hello option per attribute type.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you send a note-filled sign-up form to a neighbor, you check that they have a sticker saying they can read notes. No sticker, no notes.

sections.title: Receiving Attributes
sections.content:
A router that receives a type 1 address MUST examine all the attributes in the order they appear. Each attribute type's own specification must say what to do when several instances occur. Processing may affect how the tree is built, how other attributes of that type are handled, and whether the attribute is forwarded. If it has any such effect, the router MUST keep state tying the attribute to the adjacency it came from.

If a router does not understand an attribute type, the F-bit decides: if set, the router MUST forward the attribute, and if clear it MUST discard it. If every attribute is discarded, the router forwards a Join with a type 0 address.

Different downstream routers can send conflicting attributes of the same type. By default the router uses the attribute from the PIM adjacency with the numerically smallest IP address (the link-local address for IPv6), with the interface index as a tie breaker. It MAY remember the others so it can switch at once if the chosen adjacency is pruned or expires. A type's specification MAY define its own conflict rule, which then replaces this one. For unknown transitive attributes, the default rule applies when two adjacencies did not send byte-for-byte identical sets.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router does not know what a note means, a special mark tells it whether to pass the note along or throw it away. If two neighbors write different notes, the one from the neighbor with the smallest address wins.

sections.title: Changing the Attribute Set
sections.content:
A router may need to change the attributes for a tree because a downstream neighbor changed its set, because of attribute processing, or for reasons such as a configuration change. If its upstream neighbor stays the same, it MUST send a new Join with the new set, using a type 0 address if the new set is empty. If the upstream neighbor changes, it sends a Prune to the old one, and that Prune does not need to carry attributes.

Each Join replaces the previous attribute set entirely. There are no incremental updates: any attribute no longer present is considered withdrawn. When a downstream neighbor sends a Prune, the attributes it had sent are withdrawn, and the router may then need to send a new Join upstream with a changed set.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new sign-up form replaces the old one completely. If a note is missing from the new form, it is gone.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Option Value
sections.content:
IANA created a registry of PIM Join Attribute Types for the Attr_Type field, with assignments by the IETF Review policy. It assigned PIM Hello option value 26 to the Join Attribute option.

RFC 4601 should have created a registry for the Encoding Type field but did not, so IANA set one up referencing both documents, also with IETF Review. It defines two types: type 0, native encoding for the address family (RFC 4601), and type 1, native encoding but with zero or more PIM Join Attributes present (this RFC).
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official list of note types, so nobody makes up clashing ones. Everything on the list has to be approved first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of a Join Attribute is only as good as the security of the PIM packet carrying it, so the considerations for PIM Join packets in RFC 4601 apply. Specific attributes may add their own considerations, which must be documented in their own specifications. The RFC also notes that the security considerations of RFC 5015 (BIDIR-PIM) may apply.

The RFC also warns about deployment. A PIM router that does not understand type 1 cannot process the Join, and an attribute that affects tree construction may build the tree wrongly unless every router receiving it understands it. Attributes are therefore only useful inside a single administrative domain, or a small set of cooperating ones, where that can be determined in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes are only as safe as the envelope they travel in. Because every router must understand the notes, they work best inside one network run by people who agree on the rules.
